headline: OpenConjecture study highlights why mathematical outputs need intent and novelty review
summary: Helen Jenne, Davis Brown, Jesse He and Henry Kvinge introduce OpenConjecture, a dataset of conjectures drawn from recent mathematics preprints, and analyze a random sample of 200 conjectures from 200 papers. Across three successive GPT-model passes, the authors report proposed proofs or counterexamples for 125 items; 84% passed a review by a new instance of the same model that generated each response. The paper explicitly does not treat those outcomes as expert-verified solutions. Its analyses flag cases where counterexamples appear to exploit missing assumptions or depart from authors’ intended meaning, and where proofs follow existing results. The work argues that mathematical-agent evaluation should assess fidelity to the stated problem, relationship to prior literature, attribution and novelty, in addition to formal or literal correctness. It is a first-party, non-expert-verified study, not a measured rate of newly solved open problems.
